# Course Overview and Learning Objectives

Communication is central to how organizations function, change, and adapt. This class examines the theories, concepts, and practices that shape communication within and between organizations. We will look at how communication creates organizational culture, how power and identity operate in workplaces, and how organizations communicate with their broader environments.

Students who complete this course will be able to:

1. Understand the major theoretical traditions in organizational communication.
2. Critically analyze communication practices within organizational contexts.
3. Apply organizational communication concepts to real-world situations in their personal and professional lives.
4. Engage thoughtfully with research and scholarly perspectives on organizations.

# Course logistics

## Note About This Syllabus

Although the core expectations for this class are fixed, this is my first time teaching this course, sothe details of readings and assignments may shift based on how the class goes. As a result, there are three important things to keep in mind:

1. Although details on this syllabus will change, I will not change readings or assignments less than one week before they are due. If I don't fill in a "To Be Determined" one week before it's due, it is dropped. If you plan to read more than one week ahead, contact me first.
2. Closely monitor the class [Discord](/schedule/pages/Discord-Signup.html). I will summarize changes in announcements on Discord that should be emailed to everybody in the class if you have notifications turned on.
3. I will ask the class for voluntary anonymous feedback frequently. Please let me know what is working and what can be improved.

## Class Sessions

This course will be mostly discussion-based and application-centered. For the most part, you will engage with the content through doing readings before class, so that our time together can be used to go deeper — not to cover the basics.

**Tuesday sessions** are discussion-centric. Most of the session will be a conversation about that week's readings, driven by your questions and ideas. I will use the discussion questions from your 3-2-1 assignments to guide us. This means **I expect you to arrive on Tuesdays having done the reading.**

**Thursday sessions** are more like a workshop. We will work through case studies in groups, applying the week's concepts to real organizational scenarios. Some Thursdays will also be used for project work, peer feedback, or exams.

## Getting Help

Your first place to look for help should be each other. By asking and answering questions on Discord, you will not only help to build a repository of shared information but also reinforce our learning community.

I will also hold office hours in BRNG 2134 on Tuesdays from 1:00–3:00 PM. Come with specific questions — often just trying to articulate your confusion helps you find the answer.

I will also check Discord at least once a day. I encourage you to post questions there, and to use it as a space where we can help and instruct each other. In general, you should contact me there. I am also available by email. You can reach me at [jdfoote@purdue.edu](mailto:jdfoote@purdue.edu). I try hard to maintain a boundary between work and home and I typically respond only on weekdays during business hours.

# Assignments

There will be multiple types of assignments, designed to encourage learning in different ways.

## Participation

I expect you to be an active member of our class. This includes paying attention in class, participating in activities, and being actively engaged in learning, thinking about, and trying to understand the material.

To make sure that everyone has an opportunity to participate and to encourage you to do the assignments, I will randomly select students to discuss readings or to explain portions of homework assignments.

## Reading Review Assignments

Before most Tuesday sessions, you will complete a short reading review. Its purpose is twofold: to hold you accountable for the reading, and to surface questions that fuel our Tuesday discussion. You have two options — choose whichever works best for you on a given week.

### Option A: 3-2-1

Write and submit the following on Brightspace:

* **3** concepts you learned or connections you made from this week's reading
* **2** questions you have or things you don't fully understand
* **1** question you think would make a good class discussion question

Post your discussion question to the #discussions channel on Discord as well. Good discussion questions engage with the reading and connect it to other concepts or to the real world. For example:

* *How is organizational power different from personal authority? What are the sources of power in organizations?*
* *Would a club or a sports team be considered an organization? Why or why not?*

### Option B: AI Conversation

**After** doing the reading, open an AI tool (Claude.ai, ChatGPT, etc.) and start a conversation with a prompt like this:

> "I just read Chapter 4 of my Organizational Communication textbook about Systems and Cultural Approaches. Ask me questions and have a conversation with me to make sure I understand the most important principles and ideas."

Then have a genuine back-and-forth — answer the AI's questions, push back if something seems off, ask it to clarify things that are still fuzzy. The goal is to test your own understanding, not to receive a summary. The AI should be doing most of the asking; you should be doing most of the thinking.

Submit two things on Brightspace:

1. A shareable link to your conversation (both Claude.ai and ChatGPT support this)
2. A short reflection (a paragraph or two): Discuss what you learned from the conversation and whether you still have questions or confusions after it. 

As with the 3-2-1 assignment, post one discussion question in the #discussions channel on Discord.


## Assignments

**3-2-1 Reading Reviews** are due before most Tuesday sessions. For each, you will: write down three concepts you learned or connections you made; identify two questions or things you don't fully understand; and share one question you think would make a good class discussion. Post your discussion question to the #discussions channel on Discord. These keep you prepared for Tuesday and give me a sense of where the class is before we meet.

**In-class case studies** happen most Thursdays. In groups, you will analyze a real organizational scenario using the week's concepts and briefly share your analysis with the class. These are completed in class — no outside preparation required beyond having done the reading.

**Theory Application Short Paper** (~2 pages): Choose one concept or theory we've covered and find a real-world example from your own experience or current events that illustrates it. Explain the concept and analyze how your example demonstrates it. Due Thu, Oct 22.

**Organizational Profile / Site Selection Memo** (~1–2 pages): Identify the organization you will analyze for your final project. Describe it briefly, explain why you chose it, and identify 2–3 course concepts you think will be most useful for analyzing its communication. Due Thu, Nov 12.

**Self-Assessment Reflections** (3×): At three points during the semester you will reflect in writing on your learning, your participation, and your growth as an organizational communicator. These inform the self-assessment grading process described below. Due Oct 1, Nov 19, and Dec 10.

## Exams

There will be two in-class exams:

* **Exam 1 (Thu, Oct 8)** — covers Unit 1: approaches to organizational communication (Chs. 1–6)
* **Exam 2 (Tue, Dec 1)** — covers Unit 2: organizational communication processes (Chs. 7–12)

Exams will include a mix of concept identification, short answer, and application questions.

## Final Project

The final project is an **Organizational Communication Analysis**. You will write a 4–5 page paper analyzing the communication of an organization you belong to or have belonged to. The paper should apply at least two theoretical frameworks from the course, identify a key communication dynamic or challenge you've observed, and reflect on your own role as a communicator in that organization. You will also give a short presentation (5–7 minutes) during the last week of class. Full guidelines will be posted on Brightspace. Due Thu, Dec 10.

# Grades

This course will follow a "self-assessment" philosophy. I am more interested in helping you to learn things that will be useful to you than in assigning grades. In general, I think that my time is much better spent in providing better feedback and in being available to work through problems together.

The university still requires grades, so you will be leading the evaluation of your work. This will be completed with me in three stages: Oct 1, Nov 19, and Dec 10. In each stage, you will use [this form](/assignments/Self-Assessment-Reflection.qmd) to reflect on what you have accomplished thus far, how it has met, not met, or exceeded expectations, based on the grade-level descriptions below and your own personal goals and objectives. At each of these stages, you will receive feedback on your assessments. By the end of the semester, you should have a clear vision of your accomplishments and growth, which you will turn into a grade. As the instructor-of-record, I maintain the right to disagree with your assessment and alter grades as I see fit, but any time that I do this it will be accompanied by an explanation and discussion. These personal assessments, reflecting both honest and meaningful reflection of your work, will be the most important factor in final grades.

We will use the following rubric in our assessment:

* 25%: Participation (attendance, 3-2-1s, in-class case studies, and engagement in discussions)
* 15%: Assignments (Theory Application Short Paper, Organizational Profile memo, Self-Assessment Reflections)
* 15%: Exam 1
* 15%: Exam 2
* 30%: Final Project (paper + presentation)

The two exams will be graded like normal exams and together make up 30% of your grade. For everything else (the other 70%), I will provide feedback that informs an ongoing conversation about your work through the self-assessment process.

My interpretation of grade levels (A, B, C, D/F) is the following:

**A:** Reflects work that exceeds expectations on multiple fronts and to a great degree. Students reaching this level of achievement will:

* Do what it takes to learn the principles and concepts of organizational communication, including looking to outside sources if necessary.
* Read all of the assigned readings and work to understand how they fit with other concepts from the class and other classes.
* Come to class every day, having done the background work. Be an active, engaged participant in our discussions.
* Engage thoughtfully with an ambitious final project.
* Take intellectual risks, offering interpretations based on synthesizing material and asking for feedback from peers.
* Share work early, allowing extra time for engagement with others.
* Write reflections that grapple meaningfully with lessons learned as well as challenges.
* Complete all homework assignments at a high level.

**B:** Reflects strong work. Work at this level will be of consistently high quality. Students reaching this level of achievement will:

* Be more safe or consistent than the work described above.
* Ask meaningful questions of peers and engage them in fruitful discussion.
* Exceed requirements, but in fairly straightforward ways.
* Compose complete and sufficiently detailed reflections.
* Complete the homework assignments, almost always at a high level.

**C:** This reflects meeting the minimum expectations of the course. Students reaching this level of achievement will:

* Turn in and complete the final project on time.
* Be collegial and continue discussion, through asking simple or limited questions.
* Compose reflections with straightforward and easily manageable goals and/or avoid discussions of challenges.
* Not complete all homework assignments or complete them in a hasty or incomplete manner.

**D/F:** These are reserved for cases in which students do not complete work or participate. Students may also be impeding the ability of others to learn.

# Policies

## Attendance

I try very hard to make our meeting times valuable to you and I expect that you attend. That being said, I know that people get sick, things come up, etc. If you need to miss class, then it is your responsibility to seek out support from classmates for notes, handouts, and other information.

Only I can excuse a student from a course requirement or responsibility. When conflicts can be anticipated, such as for many University-sponsored activities and religious observations, please inform me of the situation as far in advance as possible. For unanticipated or emergency conflicts, when advance notification is not possible, contact me as soon as possible on Discord or by email. In cases of bereavement, quarantine, or isolation, the student or the student's representative should contact the Office of the Dean of Students via email or phone at 765-494-1747. Our course on Brightspace includes a link to the Dean of Students under 'Campus Resources.'

## Classroom Discussions and Peer Feedback

Throughout the course, you may receive, read, collaborate, and/or comment on classmates' work. These assignments are for class use only. You may not share them with anybody outside of class without explicit written permission from the document's author and pertaining to the specific piece.

It is essential to the success of this class that all participants feel comfortable discussing questions, thoughts, ideas, fears, reservations, apprehensions, and confusion. Therefore, you may not create any audio or video recordings during class time nor share verbatim comments with those not in class linked to people's identities unless you get clear and explicit permission. If you want to share general impressions or specifics of in-class discussions with those not in class, please do so without disclosing personal identities or details.

## Academic Integrity

While I encourage collaboration, I expect that any work that you submit is your own. Basic guidelines for Purdue students are outlined [here](https://www.purdue.edu/odos/osrr/academic-integrity/index.html), but I expect you to be exemplary members of the academic community. Please get in touch if you have any questions or concerns.

### AI Policy

Academic integrity also applies to AI. I am a technology optimist, and an AI optimist. I think AI can be an amazing tool for education and learning, but it can also be misused. The principle I expect you to follow is that you can't (and shouldn't) use AI as a **shortcut** (a tool that gives you answers). Instead, I completely support you using it as a **scaffold** (a tool that helps you think harder).

Specifically:

- **Write your own work.** Don't have AI write your reflections, essays, discussion questions, or final project prose.  You can use AI to help you brainstorm, or to give you feedback on your writing, but you should be the one doing the writing.
- **Use AI to understand topics, readings, and concepts.** Have AI explain a confusing passage, ask it to define terms, treat it like a patient tutor.
- **Disclose substantive AI use.** I expect you to be transparent about the ways that you use AI in the class.

If you're unsure whether something crosses a line, ask me. The principle to apply: would this help me learn, or skip learning?
